findings.explanation: Sources are visited in PropertySources iteration order on every lookup. The first source returning a non-null object wins, including an empty string; a null result means “not found” and advances to the next source. A null PropertySources reference or all-null results produce null. Once a non-null source value is found, nested processing and conversion occur in that branch and no later source is considered. A conversion result of null is returned immediately rather than restarting the search. Exceptions from a PropertySource or any subsequent processing, logging, or conversion are uncaught and abort the lookup, so later sources are not tried. Resolved property values are not cached; each lookup queries the current sources again.

Ordinary String and typed lookups enable nested-placeholder processing. Every retrieved String is eligible, regardless of the requested target type. A non-String CharSequence is eligible only when the requested type is exactly String or CharSequence; other values, and a CharSequence requested as another type such as StringBuilder, bypass this step. Processing order is source retrieval, eligible nested-placeholder resolution, logging, then target-type conversion. Placeholder resolution uses getPropertyAsRawString as its callback: “raw” disables this eager nested step but still performs source selection and conversion to String. The placeholder parser then recursively processes placeholders in that returned String, so nested chains still resolve without the callback eagerly resolving them first.

Implicit resolution inside getProperty is strict by default because ignoreUnresolvableNestedPlaceholders initially is false; setting it true preserves an unresolved placeholder in literal form. Explicit resolvePlaceholders is always non-strict, while resolveRequiredPlaceholders is always strict, independently of that nested-value flag. An empty retrieved String is returned immediately; explicit empty strings also remain empty. Null explicit inputs are rejected with IllegalArgumentException by the placeholder helper. Non-strict handling suppresses only the absence of a placeholder value (after any inline fallback is unavailable) by retaining the placeholder text. It does not catch exceptions thrown by source/raw lookup or conversion, and circular-placeholder detection still throws. The strict and non-strict helper objects are initialized lazily and retained, but resolved values are not cached.

setConversionService installs the exact non-null service and replaces any previously initialized one. getConversionService lazily creates, stores, and thereafter returns an independent configurable DefaultConversionService; merely calling it therefore makes that instance the service used by later lookups. Without such a configured/initialized service, conversion first returns the original object unchanged when it is already assignable to the target type; otherwise it uses DefaultConversionService.getSharedInstance(). With a configured service, that service is called directly even for an assignable value. Its result is returned as-is, including null. Conversion exceptions propagate without trying the shared service, a later source, or another conversion path. The service instance is cached, but property values and conversion results are not.

Nullable ordinary and typed retrieval return null when lookup completes without a value—or when processing a winning non-null source value ultimately returns null. Default-valued overloads first perform the full ordinary/typed lookup and use the supplied default only if that completed call returns null. Thus a conversion service returning null after a source has won causes the API default to be used, but does not cause later sources to be searched. Required overloads run the same lookup and convert any returned null, including a post-conversion null, into IllegalStateException. None of these wrappers catches source, placeholder, logging, or conversion exceptions: such failures propagate directly, with neither later sources nor API defaults tried, and required lookup does not replace them with its missing-key exception.
